scenes.title: Poetry and History
scenes.summary: The poet tells what could happen, the historian what has happened; Herodotus in verse would still be history. Poetry is more philosophical and more serious, speaking of universals, history of particulars: what Alcibiades did and suffered.

scenes.title: Names
scenes.summary: Comedy builds its plot and then gives names; tragedy keeps to real names, because what has happened is plainly possible. Yet Agathon's Antheus invents everything and pleases, and the traditional stories are known to few.

scenes.title: A Maker of Plots
scenes.summary: The poet must be a maker of plots rather than of verses; if he takes what happened, he is still its maker.

scenes.title: Episodic Plots
scenes.summary: Episodic plots, whose episodes follow without probability or necessity, are the worst; bad poets write them for themselves, good poets for the actors.

scenes.title: The Marvelous
scenes.summary: Fear and pity come most when events happen against expectation but because of one another, as when the statue of Mitys at Argos fell on his murderer.
